newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Three buyers seen for Belgian Clabecq.
newsitem.headline: Three buyers seen for Belgian Clabecq.

text.p: Three groups including an international steel firm have expressed an interest in taking over bankrupt Belgiian steel firm Forges de Clabecq.

Steel industry holding company Societe Wallonne de la Siderurgie (SWS), which holds the Belgian region of Wallonia's controlling stake in Clabecq, told Belgian television the international firm had been given an exclusive right to negotiate a takeover deal for two months.
It did not name the potential buyers. The other two were described as "a Brazilian and a European group."

SWS president Pierre Lemercinier told RTBF television that the international firm was a serious contender. "We did not expect many buyers...their level of seriousness was such that we should allow them to explore the dossier with us."
He said the firm was looking to keep Clabecq as an integrated steel maker.
Receiver Dominique Jossart told the Belga news agency on Thursday the receivers had not been told of potential buyers.

Meetings were planned for next week between businessman Roberto Grosso, acting as an emissary for the unnamed international firm, and FGTB Clabecq union leader Roberto D'Orazio, who has been leading the fight to preserve jobs at Clabecq. The firm was also carrying out a feasibility study.
There have been several demonstrations, some violent, by Clabecq workers in Brussels and at the steel works itself near the town of Tubize about 30 km south of the Belgian capital.
Clabecq was declared bankrupt in January when Wallonia pulled the plug, threatening its 1,800 workers.
Receivers, whose efforts to put together a rescue package failed when the main creditor banks refused to take part, focused on finding a buyer for the firm as a going concern.
Clabecq's death sentence was signed in December when the European Commission rejected a regional aid plan, brandishing it inadmissible state aid for a firm without a future.
Saddled with high costs, poor margins and low-quality products, Clabecq had strugged to survive in a cyclical industry marked by overcapacity and cheap imports from eastern Europe.

Other Belgian steel firms have been cool on the idea of a cooperation or merger with Clabecq, either because they are not interested in its products -- mainly heavy plate -- or because they have already found another partner.
